rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition supplies reify from a saved top-variable marker in the binding context to a typed index in the use context, as described in the paper.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition gives reify for any guest type, taking a top-variable marker in the binding context to an index of that same type in the use context.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal identity-context reification sends the unique top-variable marker to Top, exactly as in the displayed equation.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal instance has the same equation: reifying into the extended context applies Pop to the reification into the smaller context. The Haskell instance also states the context shape as a separate equality constraint, which the formal instance places in its head instead.

rows.fidelity_note: For equal binding and use contexts, the formal definition sends the saved top-variable marker to Top, exactly as the passage describes.
rows.name: instReifyIndexRefl

rows.fidelity_note: Given reification into a context, the formal definition reifies into that context extended by one type by adding one Pop to the result.
rows.name: instReifyIndexSnoc

rows.fidelity_note: The formal instance turns a conversion into one context into a conversion into that context extended by one type, adding one Pop to its result. Each extension of the context therefore contributes one Pop.
rows.name: instReifyIndexSnoc

rows.fidelity_note: The paper postpones the context-shape equality until after Haskell selects the recursive instance. The formal definition instead places the extended context directly in the instance head, so it does not implement that selection strategy.
rows.name: instReifyIndexSnoc

rows.fidelity_note: The formal contextual-variable constructor combines a saved marker with reification from its binding context into its use context, preserving the guest type.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal contextual-abstraction constructor receives a function from the newest variable’s marker to a body in the extended context, yielding a function term in the original context.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal contextual unit constructor produces a term of type Unit in any context, matching CStar.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition gives contextual terms whose abstractions receive a singleton marker for the binding context and whose variables carry reification into their use context, matching the described construction.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal conversion sends the contextual unit term to the first-order unit term, exactly as in this equation.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal conversion sends the first-order unit term to the contextual unit term, exactly as in this equation.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition translates every contextual term to a first-order term with the same context and guest type. This is the type-safe conversion claimed here; its existence does not require the closed world assumption.

rows.fidelity_note: For a contextual variable, the formal definition applies its stored reification to its saved marker and constructs a first-order variable from the resulting index.
rows.name: unembed

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition translates each first-order term to a contextual term in the same context and of the same guest type, case by case as in Fig. 2. That the two translations are mutually inverse is stated by the separate round-trip theorems.

rows.fidelity_note: In the abstraction case, the formal definition builds a contextual abstraction whose function ignores its marker argument and recursively translates the first-order body.
rows.name: contextualise

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition packages a hidden binding context, its top-variable marker, and reification into the fixed use context, matching the existential variable package described here.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition packages a hidden binding context, a marker at that context, and reification into the given use context, exactly as the displayed existential variable definition does.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal Pop branch first converts the smaller index and then extends the package’s use context by one entry, matching this equation.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition handles each Pop by converting the remaining index and then extending the resulting variable package’s use context by one entry.

rows.fidelity_note: The passage claims an isomorphism; this formal statement proves only that unembedding after contextualisation returns every original first-order term. The reverse equation is supplied by the other cited theorem.

rows.fidelity_note: The passage claims an isomorphism; this formal statement proves only that contextualisation after unembedding returns every original contextual term. Its proof uses the closed world assumption disclosed later in this subsection; the other cited theorem supplies the opposite direction.
rows.name: isoR

rows.fidelity_note: The passage names an isomorphism of variable representations; this formal statement gives one direction: converting any index to a package and reifying it returns that index.
rows.name: indexIsoL

rows.fidelity_note: The passage names an isomorphism of variable representations; this formal statement gives the reverse direction: reifying a package and converting the index back returns the original package. Its proof uses the closed world assumption.
rows.name: indexIsoR

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement is the displayed equation $\operatorname{unembed}(\operatorname{contextualise}(e))=e$ for every first-order term, in any context and at any guest type; its proof does not use the closed world assumption.
rows.name: isoL

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement is the displayed equation $\operatorname{contextualise}(\operatorname{unembed}(e))=e$ for every contextual term. Its proof uses the closed world assumption discussed immediately below, so equality of the displayed statements does not mean an assumption-free isomorphism.
rows.name: isoR

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement gives the left-inverse equation discussed under this heading: reifying the variable package produced from any index returns the original index. It does not require the closed world assumption.
rows.name: indexIsoL

rows.fidelity_note: The passage describes proof by induction; the formal statement says that reifying the package produced from an index returns that index. The supplied proof does use induction on the index, but that proof method is not a separate theorem statement.
rows.name: indexIsoL

rows.fidelity_note: The passage explains how weakening and reification cancel at each Pop; the formal statement gives the resulting equality for the entire index. The supplied inductive proof follows this explanation, rather than stating a separate step-count theorem.
rows.name: indexIsoL

rows.fidelity_note: The formal theorem gives the reverse variable round trip. Reify the saved marker with the package’s stored instance, then convert the resulting index back to recover the original package and its instance. The proof uses the closed world assumption introduced next in the paper.
rows.name: indexIsoR

rows.fidelity_note: The formal assumption says every reification instance is either the identity-context instance or a one-entry extension of another instance. This is the paper’s closed world condition, assumed here rather than derived from instance resolution.
rows.name: closedWorld

rows.fidelity_note: The passage justifies the assumption by hiding a type class from users; the formal declaration simply assumes the two-case condition for every reification instance. It does not prove that a module boundary enforces that condition.
rows.name: closedWorld

rows.fidelity_note: The passage describes the proof: case analysis on the reification instances, made possible by the closed world assumption. The formal statement is the resulting reverse round-trip equation; its proof does split on the two cases that assumption allows and recurses through the extension case.
rows.name: indexIsoR

rows.fidelity_note: The passage names the variable case’s proof dependency; the formal statement gives the first-order term round-trip equation. Its variable case does use the index round-trip result, as the passage says.
rows.name: isoL

rows.fidelity_note: The passage names the contextual-variable case’s proof dependency; the formal statement gives the contextual term round-trip equation. Its proof uses the reverse variable round trip and therefore the closed world assumption.
rows.name: isoR

rows.fidelity_note: The passage describes the abstraction case’s use of function extensionality; the formal statement gives the contextual term round-trip equation. The supplied proof uses extensionality and the singleton marker to establish equality of the abstraction bodies.
rows.name: isoR

rows.fidelity_note: The passage says that transferring proofs between the two representations relies on the round-trip results and so on the closed world assumption. This direction, unembedding after contextualisation returns the first-order term, is proved without that assumption; only the reverse direction uses it.
rows.name: isoL

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement says that contextualising after unembedding returns the original contextual term, and its proof does use the closed world assumption, as the passage says. The passage concerns how proofs transfer between representations, which no formal statement here expresses.
rows.name: isoR
